questions.label: Q1(d)
questions.sharedContext:
Computer Arithmetic & Algebraic Equations

Consider the quadratic polynomial $p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a = 0.51$, $b = 1.96$, and $c = -0.05$.
questions.text: (d) Which formula do you prefer for this root, and why?
questions.modelAnswer:
The alternative formula is preferred for this root.

In the standard formula, the numerator $-b + \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}$ subtracts two nearly equal numbers, $-1.96 + 1.98$, causing cancellation and loss of significant digits. The alternative formula avoids this cancellation by using addition in the denominator, giving a much smaller relative error.

questions.label: Q4(a)
questions.text: (a) Approximate $\int_1^3 f(x)\,dx$ using Simpson’s rule for the given data.
questions.modelAnswer:
Here $h = 0.5$ and there are four subintervals. Simpson’s rule gives

$$\int_1^3 f(x)\,dx \approx \frac{h}{3}\left(f_0 + f_4 + 4(f_1+f_3) + 2f_2\right).$$

Substituting the data:

$$\int_1^3 f(x)\,dx \approx \frac{0.5}{3}\left(0.84+0.42+4(1.52+1.48)+2(1.82)\right).$$

$$= \frac{0.5}{3}(16.90) = 2.816666\ldots$$

Therefore

$$\int_1^3 f(x)\,dx \approx 2.817.$$

questions.label: Q4(b)
questions.text: (b) How would you expect the accuracy of your result to improve if you were to use Simpson’s rule with a spacing of $0.1$ between the data points?
questions.modelAnswer:
Composite Simpson’s rule has error of order $O(h^4)$.

Changing the spacing from $h = 0.5$ to $h = 0.1$ reduces $h$ by a factor of $5$, so the error is expected to decrease by a factor of

$$5^4 = 625.$$ 

Thus the result should be about $625$ times more accurate, assuming the function is sufficiently smooth.

questions.label: Q4(c)
questions.text: (c) Using the most accurate $3$-point difference formula available, give approximations of $f'(1.0)$ and $f'(2.5)$.
questions.modelAnswer:
The spacing is $h = 0.5$.

At $x=1.0$, use the three-point forward difference formula:

$$f'(1.0) \approx \frac{-3f(1.0)+4f(1.5)-f(2.0)}{2h}.$$ 

$$f'(1.0) \approx \frac{-3(0.84)+4(1.52)-1.82}{1.0} = 1.74.$$ 

At $x=2.5$, use the three-point central difference formula:

$$f'(2.5) \approx \frac{f(3.0)-f(2.0)}{2h}.$$ 

$$f'(2.5) \approx \frac{0.42-1.82}{1.0} = -1.40.$$

questions.label: Q5(a)
questions.text:
Least-Squares Approximation

(a) Briefly explain the significance of the fast Fourier transform for large-scale signal processing, including a discussion of the computational complexity.
questions.modelAnswer:
The fast Fourier transform is significant because it computes the discrete Fourier transform much more efficiently than direct evaluation.

A direct computation of the discrete Fourier transform for $n$ data points requires $O(n^2)$ arithmetic operations. The fast Fourier transform reduces this to $O(n\log n)$ operations. For large-scale signal processing this makes Fourier analysis practical, since very large data sets can be transformed, filtered, compressed, and analysed much faster.

questions.label: Q5(b)
questions.text:
(b) Compute the second approximations $s_2$ of the discrete Fourier transform for the following $n = 8$ data points over the time interval $[0,2\pi]$:

| $t_j$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{4}\pi$ | $\frac{1}{2}\pi$ | $\frac{3}{4}\pi$ | $\pi$ | $\frac{5}{4}\pi$ | $\frac{3}{2}\pi$ | $\frac{7}{4}\pi$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $y_j$ | $3.42$ | $3.20$ | $1.16$ | $1.80$ | $4.46$ | $3.83$ | $1.16$ | $1.51$ |
questions.modelAnswer:
For $n=8$, the trigonometric least-squares approximation of degree $2$ is

$$s_2(t)=\frac{a_0}{2}+a_1\cos t+b_1\sin t+a_2\cos(2t)+b_2\sin(2t).$$

Using

$$a_k=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}y_j\cos(kt_j), \quad b_k=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}y_j\sin(kt_j),$$

we obtain

$$a_0 = \frac{2}{8}(3.42+3.20+1.16+1.80+4.46+3.83+1.16+1.51)=5.135,$$

$$a_1 = 0.5023, \quad b_1 = 0.4220,$$

$$a_2 = 1.3900, \quad b_2 = 0.4925.$$ 

Therefore

$$s_2(t)=2.5675+0.5023\cos t+0.4220\sin t+1.3900\cos(2t)+0.4925\sin(2t).$$

questions.label: Q5(c)
questions.text: (c) What is the strongest frequency present in the signal?
questions.modelAnswer:
The amplitudes of the frequency components are

$$A_1 = \sqrt{a_1^2+b_1^2} = \sqrt{0.5023^2+0.4220^2} \approx 0.656,$$

$$A_2 = \sqrt{a_2^2+b_2^2} = \sqrt{1.3900^2+0.4925^2} \approx 1.475.$$ 

The strongest frequency present in the signal is therefore frequency $2$.

questions.label: Q6(a)
questions.text:
Linear Algebra

(a) State the Gershgorin circle theorem.
questions.modelAnswer:
For an $n \times n$ matrix $A=(a_{ij})$, every eigenvalue of $A$ lies in at least one of the Gershgorin discs

$$D_i = \left\{z \in \mathbb{C}: |z-a_{ii}| \leq \sum_{j\neq i}|a_{ij}|\right\}, \quad i=1,\ldots,n.$$ 

Equivalently, the spectrum of $A$ is contained in the union of these discs.

questions.label: Q6(b)
questions.text: (b) Apply one step of the QR method to $A$.
questions.modelAnswer:
First compute a QR factorisation $A=QR$.

The columns of $A$ are

$$a_1=\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\end{pmatrix}, \quad a_2=\begin{pmatrix}5\\7\end{pmatrix}.$$ 

Then

$$q_1=\frac{a_1}{\|a_1\|}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0.8\\0.6\end{pmatrix},$$

and an orthogonal vector is

$$q_2=\begin{pmatrix}-0.6\\0.8\end{pmatrix}.$$ 

Thus

$$Q=\begin{pmatrix}0.8 & -0.6\\0.6 & 0.8\end{pmatrix}.$$ 

Now

$$R=Q^TA=\begin{pmatrix}0.8 & 0.6\\-0.6 & 0.8\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}4&5\\3&7\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5 & 8.2\\0 & 2.6\end{pmatrix}.$$ 

One step of the QR method gives

$$A_1=RQ=\begin{pmatrix}5 & 8.2\\0 & 2.6\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0.8 & -0.6\\0.6 & 0.8\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}8.92 & 3.56\\1.56 & 2.08\end{pmatrix}.$$

questions.label: Q6(c)
questions.text: (c) Give bounds on the eigenvalues of $A$,
questions.modelAnswer:
Using Gershgorin’s theorem, the eigenvalues lie in the union of the discs

$$|\lambda-4| \leq 5,$$

$$|\lambda-7| \leq 3.$$ 

Since the matrix is real and the eigenvalues are real, this gives the interval bounds

$$\lambda \in [-1,9] \cup [4,10].$$

Thus all eigenvalues lie in

$$[-1,10].$$
